transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-11-19
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Nimbus - Head of ML), Alex Rivera (Nimbus - Platform), Priya Singh (Nimbus - Security), Jordan Lee (Nimbus PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): High-level POC scoping; customer leans toward dedicated for cost predictability but concerns about data residency and SSO; agreed to run benchmarks on their traffic; Redwood to provide detailed POC plan and pricing.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we should do quick intros then jump into the workloads and what success looks like for the POC, is that ok?
[00:07] Laura: Yep, thanks Maya. Laura here, head of ML at Nimbus. Our team runs the fraud scoring infra.
[00:10] Alex: Alex, infra/platform, I'll be managing the networking and infra side.
[00:13] Priya: Priya on security, I'll look at compliance/KMS and SSO stuff.
[00:17] Diego: Hi all, Diego SE from Redwood, I'll scope the benchmarks and perf details.
[00:22] Jordan: Jordan, PM, helping coordinate timelines.
[00:25] Maya: Cool. Quick context - you mentioned in the form you want an online scoring endpoint for transaction risk, about 200 qps peak, 30 req/s steady with p95 latency target sub-120ms, and data residency in us-west. Is that still right?
[00:37] Laura: Yes that's the general shape. Our current infra is log-based scoring then real-time model; want to move model to a central inference service. We care a lot about P95 and tail. Cost per 1M requests is a big factor too — we have to justify spend.
[00:49] Alex: Also we can't have raw PII leave our VPC, so either a Private deployment or dedicated with VPC peering is preferable. Hosted could work if data is masked but we prefer not to re-architect.
[01:03] Priya: From compliance, SOC2 plus our internal PCI-lite controls. Need audit logs, KMS integration for key management, and SSO (SAML) for ops access.
[01:12] Diego: Noted. For the POC we typically run three tracks: 1) hosted baseline to validate model accuracy and latency on sample traffic, 2) dedicated reserved capacity to mirror production throughput and give cost numbers, and 3) private (VPC or on-prem) for compliance gating. We can scope the depth of each depending on priority.
[01:27] Laura: We're trying to decide which to prioritize. Our immediate ask is to validate latency and p95 tail, then cost. If hosted proves we hit latency and tail, maybe we can accept it if we don't have to send raw PII.
[01:38] Maya: Right, typical decision criteria we recommend: 1) latency and tail SLOs, 2) data residency / security controls, 3) cost predictability, and 4) operational ownership. Hosted is fastest to iterate, Dedicated gives predictable throughput and isolation, Private gives maximum control but longer lead time.
[01:54] Alex: Can you unpack dedicated a bit — does that live in our VPC or in Redwood-managed infra?
[01:58] Diego: Dedicated is in a Redwood-managed cluster but we give you a private tenancy and network isolation. You can do VPC peering, private endpoints, and we support customer-managed KMS in many cases. It's not in your VPC (unless we do a private deployment), but network isolation and egress controls are available.
[02:16] Alex: So egress still touches Redwood's infra. For us that matters because we have to maintain PCI boundaries.
[02:21] Priya: Yes, we need an answer on whether PII ever lands unencrypted on Redwood nodes, and how KMS unwraps are handled.
[02:29] Diego: For dedicated we can support envelope encryption with customer KMS; keys never leave your control. Unwrapped payloads may be present in memory on the instance during inference — we can apply memory encryption and strict retention windows. For private, all compute runs in your environment and we never see unencrypted payload.
[02:46] Maya: Practical POC flow: we run a hosted baseline using a Redwood-verified model variant (or your model if you bring one), capture performance signals, then run a dedicated benchmark to validate throughput and cost, and optionally a private deploy for compliance sign-off. Typical timeline 3-6 weeks depending on private deployment lead time.
[03:03] Jordan: 3-6 weeks — can you break that down? We have a Q4 go/no-go in early Dec.
[03:09] Diego: Sure. Hosted baseline + functional validation: 1 week. Dedicated benchmark and cost modeling: 1-2 weeks. Private deployment (if needed) provisioning + security review: 2-4 weeks depending on network approvals. So end-to-end could be 4-7 weeks, but we can parallelize some items.
[03:26] Laura: For the hosted baseline, what data do you need? We can't send PII.
[03:30] Diego: Sample traffic with synthetic or hashed PII is fine. We mainly need token length distribution, seq length, request rate pattern, and representative payloads to exercise the model. Also the model blob if you're bringing your own.
[03:43] Laura: We'll scrub PII and provide a synthetic dataset and traces.
[03:46] Priya: Also need to see SOC2 report and how RBAC/Audit logs are surfaced.
[03:51] Maya: We'll attach SOC2 + ISO artifacts and a security brief. For audit logs we expose per-request metadata and you can push logs to your SIEM via syslog or S3.
[03:59] Alex: On performance, Diego, can you outline what you'll measure in the benchmark?
[04:03] Diego: Absolutely — key metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tail latency distribution, tokens/sec, concurrency vs throughput curve, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rates (if using prefix caching), and cost per 1M tokens. We'll also track cold-start behavior and steady-state behavior.
[04:20] Laura: Our p95 target is 120ms; p99 ideally under 300ms. We want 200 qps peak. Does that map to GPU-backed inference?
[04:27] Diego: Likely yes — to hit p95 120ms with your model family we'll probably use GPU-backed serving with batching tuned for low-latency. There's a tradeoff: tighter batching improves throughput and cost but increases latency. We'll test batching knobs to find a sweet spot.
[04:40] Jordan: Any allowances for autoscaling bursts? We have traffic spikes during promotions.
[04:44] Diego: Yes, our dedicated offering supports burst capacity and autoscaling policies. For hosted we have scaling too but it's multi-tenant and may impact cost predictability.
[04:52] Maya: One mis-transcription note — I think our internal docs call KV cache "key-vee cache" but sometimes transcripts show it oddly, just flagging.
[04:58] Diego: ha, yep Fireflies likes to make it weird.
[05:01] Priya: On encryption, we need confirmation on envelope encryption, where KMS CMKs are stored, and whether Redwood will have access to plaintext logs.
[05:10] Diego: We'll send an architecture note: for dedicated with customer KMS, Redwood orchestrates calls to your KMS for key unwrap. We don't persist plaintext to disk; logs are redacted unless you opt-in to full request logging. For private deploy, no keys leave your environment.
[05:25] Alex: For the POC can we run an initial hosted baseline to validate tail latency and accuracy, then run dedicated with our KMS to prove cost and throughput?
[05:31] Maya: That's our recommended path; it gives quickest signal, then full validation for production constraints.
[05:35] Laura: Sounds good. Two concerns: 1) How long until dedicated capacity is available? 2) Cost modeling accuracy.
[05:41] Diego: Dedicated provisioning is typically a few days to a week for small pools, up to longer for large reserved clusters. For cost we run a token-level simulation using your traffic profile to estimate per-1M request costs across configurations (quantization, batch sizes, instance types). We'll share a spreadsheet.
[05:57] Jordan: Great, what are the acceptance criteria for the POC?
[06:00] Maya: Suggested acceptance criteria: 1) meet p95 <120ms on representative traffic for >95% of runs; 2) cost per 1M requests within X% of budget (TBD); 3) security checklist items satisfied (KMS integration, audit logs); 4) runbook for failover and rollback validated. We'll write this into the POC plan.
[06:18] Priya: Add: penetration test or security review window before private go-live.
[06:22] Diego: Good call. We'll add PT scope for the private route.
[06:25] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps: Redwood to send detailed POC plan, pricing spreadsheet, SOC2/ISO artifacts, and benchmark template. Nimbus to send synthetic dataset, traffic profile, and compliance questionnaire answers. Schedule benchmark next Wednesday — does that work?
[06:37] Laura: Yes Wed 11/26 works for the team.
[06:39] Maya: Perfect. Any final questions?
[06:42] Alex: One small one — are there any caveats around model variants/quantization impacting accuracy?
[06:46] Diego: Quantization can reduce memory and cost but can affect model quality. We'll include head-to-head evals in the benchmark: float32 vs int8/quantized variants so you can see tradeoffs.
[06:56] Laura: Great. Thanks everyone.
[06:58] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the plan and send calendar invites for the bench runs.
[07:02] Priya: Thanks.
[07:04] (meeting ends)
